A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VerifyBench research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original verifier evaluations, reference-answer ablations, error analyses, and rejection-sampling fine-tuning results in Tables 2–5 and Figure 3.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds evaluations of further verifiers in Table 2 and direct reinforcement-learning experiments in Section 5.2 and Appendix H.1.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction pipeline, answer categories, verification prompts, balancing procedure, and five-model disagreement filtering remain unchanged. The meta-annotator description expands the existing adjudication procedure. GRPO is introduced as an evaluation experiment rather than a proposed method component.

E1.justification: v3 adds AMC23 and MinervaMath as downstream evaluation datasets. The 41 benchmark-construction sources and the original GSM8K, MATH500, and SVAMP evaluations remain. Coverage expands within mathematical reasoning while the benchmark domains and answer types stay unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds DeepSeek-V3-0324, DeepSeek-R1-0528, gpt-oss-20b, gpt-oss-120b, and seven dedicated verifiers across xVerify, Tencent-Qwen2.5-7B-RLVR, and CompassVerifier. This substantially broadens comparison beyond the original rule-based method and general LLM judges. Existing comparators, including Table 4's reward models, are retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds GRPO training of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on DeepMath-103K, using four verifier conditions, 16 rollouts per query, and checkpoint evaluation every ten steps. Appendix H.1 specifies the new training and evaluation settings. The original rejection-sampling protocol is retained in H.2, rather than replaced.

E4.justification: Section 5.2 adds direct RL validation of whether verifier benchmark performance predicts downstream training outcomes, including deterioration under weaker verifiers. This substantially extends the original rejection-sampling correlation analysis. The reference-answer ablation and fine-grained error analysis remain unchanged; the taxonomy table redisplays existing categories.

E5.justification: Appendix H.1 newly specifies eight stochastic generations per test example for the RL evaluation. The retained rejection-sampling evaluation still averages sixteen generations, as in v1. This adds repeat-count information for the new experiment without establishing additional independent training runs; neither version reports training-seed uncertainty or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial verifier results and RL learning curves. Table 2's highest reported VerifyBench-Hard accuracy changes from 72.60% for GPT-4o in v1 to 87.90% for gpt-oss-120b and CompassVerifier-32B in v3 through added model entries. Shared table results and the original rejection-sampling curves remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 retain the same reward mappings and accuracy definitions; changing Acc to Accuracy is not substantive. No new theoretical assumptions, theorems, or proofs are introduced. Table 8 restates the taxonomy already documented in v1's classification prompt.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: reference-based verification needs dedicated evaluation, VerifyBench-Hard exposes difficult cases, and benchmark performance can guide reasoning-model training. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds the interpretation that weak verifiers can degrade RL-trained models through biased reward assignment and inaccurate supervision; v1 emphasized better rejection-sampling outcomes with stronger verifiers. The five limitations remain substantively unchanged in Appendix A. Appendix C newly states that general reasoning includes commonsense subsets, conflicting with the retained domain limitation.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility information: annotator qualifications, training, instructions and interfaces; benchmark-generation sampling settings; source-split handling; and detailed RL software, hyperparameters, hardware, evaluation, and smoothing procedures. It also adds code and project-page links. These disclosures accompany retention of the original rejection-sampling implementation details.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds substantive positioning against concurrent reference-based verification work, especially VerifierBench. It acknowledges similar construction and distinguishes VerifyBench through 41 versus 14 sources, finer annotation, disagreement-based hard-case selection, and reasoning-model outputs. Discussion of dedicated model-based verifiers also expands the earlier emphasis on preference and process reward systems.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the section sequence remain intact. Section 5.2 is rewritten around RL, the original rejection-sampling discussion moves to Appendix H.2, and limitations move to Appendix A. Appendix organization, explanatory passages, terminology, and affiliation text receive localized revisions.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to predominantly single-column formatting, with extensive table and figure repositioning. v3 expands Table 2, adds annotation-interface screenshots and RL plots, and redisplays the taxonomy as Table 8. The original RFT plot becomes Figure 10, while existing examples receive larger, less abbreviated displays.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's practical validation by adding direct GRPO experiments where v1 relied on rejection-sampling fine-tuning. Dedicated-verifier comparisons and detailed annotation and implementation documentation also address important evaluation and reproducibility gaps. The retained 72.4% maximum claim now conflicts sharply with Table 2's 87.90%, and some documentation remains inconsistent, but these defects do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.
